Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Expectation2: Prepare sermons and deliver weekly messages during Shabbat services.
Situation2: The regular weekly Shabbat service is approaching.
Story: I glance at my phone and see the message from Eli, my oldest friend. His words are clipped, his tone wounded. He’s misunderstood my last text, and I know I should call him right now, clear the air before the hurt festers. That’s what friends do—communicate, resolve things before they grow. But as I reach for my phone, my eyes fall on the open notebook on my desk, half-filled with scribbled sermon notes. Shabbat is only hours away, and as the rabbi, the congregation expects me to be prepared, to offer them guidance and inspiration. I can’t let them down, not when so many look to me for comfort and wisdom each week. My heart pounds as I weigh the phone in my hand, torn between the urgent need to heal a friendship and the sacred duty to my community. The minutes slip by, and I feel the pressure mounting from both sides, each role demanding my full attention, each expectation pulling me in a different direction.
